abstract: Recent multi-task learning research argues against *unitary scalarization*, where training simply minimizes the sum of the task losses. Several ad-hoc multi-task optimization algorithms have instead been proposed, inspired by various hypotheses about what makes multi-task settings difficult. The majority of these optimizers require per-task gradients, and introduce significant memory, runtime, and implementation overhead. We show that unitary scalarization, coupled with standard regularization and stabilization techniques from single-task learning, matches or improves upon the performance of complex multi-task optimizers in popular supervised and reinforcement learning settings. We then present an analysis suggesting that many specialized multi-task optimizers can be partly interpreted as forms of regularization, potentially explaining our surprising results. We believe our results call for a critical reevaluation of recent research in the area.

bibliographic.title: In Defense of the Unitary Scalarization for Deep Multi-Task Learning
bibliographic.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35 (NeurIPS 2022)

content.problem: Deep multi-task learning research increasingly argues that unitary scalarization, simply minimizing the sum of per-task losses, underperforms specialized multi-task optimizers, and the authors attribute this reported weakness to experimental variability and insufficient regularization rather than to inherent optimization difficulty.
content.proposed_solution: The authors benchmark popular specialized multi-task optimizers against unitary scalarization in a unified experimental pipeline across supervised and reinforcement learning settings, coupling the simple baseline with standard single-task regularization and stabilization techniques, and provide an empirical and technical analysis suggesting that many specialized optimizers act as regularizers.
content.algorithm_or_model: unitary scalarization coupled with standard regularization and stabilization techniques

content.claim: No specialized multi-task optimizer consistently outperforms unitary scalarization across popular supervised and reinforcement learning benchmarks once the simple baseline is combined with standard regularization and stabilization, and many specialized optimizers can be partly interpreted as forms of regularization.
author_stated_limitations: Although a wide range of popular benchmarks was covered, the authors cannot exclude the existence of settings where unitary scalarization underperforms.
Experimental results were obtained via grid searches under limited compute resources, so some of the compared methods might benefit from further fine-tuning.
The regularization hypothesis is presented only as a partial explanation of the results rather than a complete account.

evidence.problem_quote: Existing SMTOs were introduced to solve challenges related to the optimization of the deep MTL problem. We instead postulate that the reported weakness of unitary scalarization is linked to experimental variability or to a lack of regularization, leading to the following contributions:
evidence.proposed_solution_quote: We show that unitary scalarization, coupled with standard regularization and stabilization techniques from single-task learning, matches or improves upon the performance of complex multi-task optimizers in popular supervised and reinforcement learning settings.
evidence.claim_quote: Surprisingly, our evaluation showed that none of the SMTOs consistently outperform unitary scalarization, the simplest and least expensive method. Second, in order to explain our surprising results, we postulate that SMTOs act as regularizers and present an analysis that supports our hypothesis.
author_stated_limitation_quotes: While we covered a wide range of popular benchmarks, we do not exclude the existence of settings where unitary scalarization underperforms: discovering them is an interesting direction for future work.
Furthermore, our experimental results were obtained via grid searches under limited compute resources: some of the methods might benefit from further fine-tuning.
Finally, we presented the regularization hypothesis only as a partial explanation of our results: we hope it will steer further analysis and consequently improve the understanding of MTL.
